conventions: `נָשַׁךְ` in the interest laws is rendered *lend upon interest* and *lent upon interest*, and every occurrence heads on the English verb rather than on *interest*: the Hebrew verb's own lexeme is the lending, and the noun is the phrasal complement English needs in order to state it, not a bleached light verb's complement. All four occurrences are read that way — 23.19 *thou shalt not lend upon interest* and *is lent upon interest*, 23.20 *thou mayest lend upon interest* and *thou shalt not lend upon interest*. Rule 44's light-verb head was the competing reading and is named in both verses under rule 8.

An English relative adverb goes to the morpheme carrying the local or directional sense it is built on, and a connective whose sense that word does not carry is left `unrepresented` beside it. At 23.12 `שָׁמָּה` with its directive `he` takes the whole of *whither* while the waw of `וְיָצָאתָ` is `unrepresented`, because *whither* says the direction but not the coordination; at 23.16 `בְּ` takes the bare *where* of *where it pleaseth him best*, no relative or resumptive morpheme standing in that clause. Where a relative morpheme is written it joins the fusion instead, as `אֲשֶׁר ... שָׁמָּה ה` → *whither* does at 23.20 under rule 22. Rule 17's sentence giving a recast relative to the waw was the competing reading at 23.12 and is named there.
report: Checked all 35 candidate lemma groups, the three `added` units, and the dump end to end. Every bucket with more than one treatment is the ASV writing different English for one construction the chapter analysed one way; no construction is analysed two ways with nothing in the source to license the difference.

`מִחוּץ לַמַּחֲנֶה` at 23.10 (*out of the camp*) and 23.12 (*without the camp*) is one analysis with two renderings: `מִן`+`חוּץ` fused under rule 30 in both, the `לְ` `unrepresented` in both, the assimilated article taking the written *the* in both. Only the English preposition differs.

The two *whither* units are licensed by the source rather than a split. 23.20 writes `אֲשֶׁר`, a relative morpheme whose sense the word carries, so it joins the fusion under rule 22; 23.12 writes only `שָׁמָּה` with its directive `he`, and that clause's waw is `unrepresented` because *whither* carries the direction but not the waw's coordination. Both verses name the competing reading under rule 8.

`דּוֹר` + ordinal (23.2, 23.3, 23.8) is one treatment throughout: the supplied preposition and the supplied determiner both join the noun under rules 33 and 15, and the ordinal keeps only its own word. Only the preposition's English differs (*to* / *of*).

The rule 33 / rule 44 boundary for a supplied preposition holds chapter-wide: goal and appositional accusatives take the word themselves (`מַחֲנֶה` → *in camp* 23.9, `בֵּית יְהוָה` → *into the house* 23.18, `דּוֹר` 23.2/3/8, `אֲרַם נַהֲרַיִם` → *of Mesopotamia* 23.4), while `עֲנָבִים` at 23.24 — the bare direct object of *eat*, with no marker and no preposition of its own — leaves its *of* with the verb. The 23.24 note records that correction explicitly.

Compound prepositions head on the governing first morpheme in all three places regardless of the English written: `מֵעִם` → *from* (23.15) and → *of* (23.21), `מֵאַחֲרֵי` → *from* (23.14). That is rule 23's instruction not to read the source head off the translation, applied consistently.

The three `added` units are each a supplied word no morpheme licenses — *his* at 23.1 (no possessive morpheme, rule 18's closing sentence), *him* at 23.10 and *any* at 23.24 (supplied objects with no object morpheme, rule 44). Nowhere else in the chapter is a word of the same kind folded into a neighbouring unit: every supplied subject pronoun in a recast relative clause (23.20 `מִשְׁלַח`, 23.23 `מוֹצָא`, 23.13 `צֵאָה`, 23.10 `קְרֵה`) joins its clause's unit under rules 46 and 17, which is the distinction rule 44 draws.

BSB: all twelve disagreements are documented convention differences and none is a genuine error. The six `R` are prepositions the ASV's own recasting leaves nothing to say — 23.5's infinitival `לְ` after *would not hearken* (rule 52), 23.8's resumptive `לָהֶם` (rule 22), 23.10's `אֶל` standing before the compound `מִחוּץ` (rule 40), 23.12 and 23.13's possessive `לְ` in *shalt have* (rule 43), and 23.16's `לוֹ` in *where it pleaseth him best* (rule 40). The two `לַ` of `מִחוּץ לַמַּחֲנֶה` go the same way, 23.5's `אֵת` is rule 16, 23.8's `הֶם` is the suffix of the unrendered resumptive phrase, 23.13's waw is a genuinely unrendered apodosis connective (the ASV opens *thou shalt dig* bare), and 23.12's waw is the *whither* case above.

The one `noncompositional` unit, `עַל־דְּבַר אֲשֶׁר` → *because* at 23.4, is left as accepted. Rule 6's first-token fallback and rule 23's construct head are both arguable for a three-morpheme grammaticalized conjunction whose one English word writes no morpheme's lexeme; the verse note names the competing reading, and there is no corpus row for this expression to settle it.
Two conventions recorded. Nothing here generalises on the evidence available — the relative-adverb case is a single occurrence with no corpus row behind it — so no promotions and no amendments.
